articles.title: OpenAI countersues Apple and accuses it of stealing trade secrets
articles.text:
OpenAI Countersues Apple And Accuses It Of Stealing Trade Secrets
The suit suggests that the iPhone maker is trying to “compete unfairly by any means available.” Unsplash/Solen Feyissa Add Engadget on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover OpenAI has filed a major lawsuit against Apple that accuses the iPhone maker of stealing trade secrets, according to a report by Financial Times . The folks behind ChatGPT have also accused Apple of "coercing and threatening" suppliers who work with both companies. OpenAI says Apple is trying to "compete unfairly by any means available", which includes encouraging employees to store corporate files on personal devices and cloud storage accounts. The complaint is filled with flowery language that suggests "Apple set quite a trap for employees" and that "bright young minds thought they would work in Cupertino. Instead they were joining Hotel California: you can check out any time you like, but you can never leave." This follows a suit issued by Apple against OpenAI that accused the AI company of stealing secret trade information . This was filed after OpenAI acquired an entity called io , which is a studio led by Apple's former design chief Jony Ive. At that point, Apple called ChatGPT "rotten to its core." Now it looks like OpenAI is getting involved in a bit of tit for tat. Apple has yet to comment on today's lawsuit, but it wasn't that long ago in which the two companies were partnered up to bring ChatGPT to iPhones . Now OpenAI is prepping its own line of hardware products that could directly compete with Apple. To that end, the company has accused a former employee of returning to Apple and sharing details about product plans and suppliers . This is pretty much the exact same thing Apple accused OpenAI of doing in its suit. That filing names several former Apple employees and says they "surreptitiously accessed and downloaded dozens of Apple's confidential hardware-related files, including voluminous, detailed information about unreleased products, engineering presentations, technical specifications and proprietary project data." In any event, the courts will have to settle this whole thing. We'll keep you posted as these two suits make their way through the legal system.

articles.title: OpenAI countersues Apple for stealing trade secrets
articles.text:
OpenAI countersues Apple for stealing trade secrets
Livestream Menu In this article OpenAI sued Apple on Friday, accusing the Big Tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices, after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology. The ChatGPT maker filed counterclaims in California federal court on Friday, saying that Apple's employment practices were designed to "trap" employees and prevent them from working on competitors' technology. OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal electronic devices that threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf," the company said in its Friday court filing. OpenAI said in the filing that Apple gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who worked at OpenAI for six months. In that time, the employee gained access to specific information on a new device as well as OpenAI's roadmap for future hardware products. "Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place," OpenAI said. Apple denied using the rehired employee to access OpenAI's confidential information and denied trying to suppress competition in AI device manufacturing. "OpenAI's counterclaims are a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple's lawsuit," Apple said in a Friday statement. Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as the intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition for talent and proprietary technology. Apple sued OpenAI and former Apple employees Tang Tan and Chang Liu in July, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT owner's foray into consumer hardware. Tan, a 24-year Apple employee who was a vice president of product design for iPhone and Apple Watch, was part of the group that launched the AI device startup io Products before it was acquired by OpenAI in 2025. OpenAI and the employees have denied those allegations and said that Apple's lawsuit depended on its unauthorized monitoring of Liu's personal messages after he stopped working for Apple. OpenAI and attorneys for Tan and Liu did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday's court filing. In Friday's filing, OpenAI criticized Apple for encouraging employees to do work on their personal Apple devices and accounts, then preventing those employees from an orderly separation of work and personal accounts when they leave for new jobs. OpenAI said that Apple continues to access former employees' personal devices and accounts after they leave the company, enabling Apple to "monitor and ensnare departing employees" when they leave for competitors. articles.text:
Explained: What is ‘Starmind’? SpaceX gets FCC nod for 1 million space-based data centres - Full details | Company Business News
Starmind is a planned constellation of solar-powered satellites equipped with AI computing hardware. (AI enhanced image: AI1 image: https://www.spacex.com) AI Quick Read SpaceX has received approval from the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to deploy up to 1 million orbital computing modules for a proposed constellation of space-based data centres , marking a major push to take artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure beyond Earth. The project, called Starmind, is designed to harness solar energy in space to power AI computing systems, process data in orbit and transmit results back to Earth through high-speed laser links connected to the Starlink network. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr described the authorisation as a step towards strengthening America's leadership in advanced computing, saying orbital data centres could support the infrastructure needed for the country's growing super-intelligence economy. The approval comes as technology companies increasingly explore alternatives to conventional data centres, with space emerging as a potential location for future computing infrastructure. The FCC said that it had granted SpaceX the first authorisation in US history for a constellation of data centres in space. The proposed network is aimed at meeting the growing demand for computing infrastructure as AI and super-intelligence technologies expand. Starmind is a planned constellation of solar-powered satellites equipped with AI computing hardware. Instead of relying entirely on terrestrial data centres, SpaceX , a space transportation company founded by Elon Musk , intends to deploy computing infrastructure in orbit, where satellites can access solar energy without atmospheric or weather-related losses. The system is designed to process AI workloads in space and beam the results back to Earth through optical laser connections and the Starlink network. SpaceX believes orbital data centres could help overcome some of the constraints faced by conventional data centres, including electricity shortages, land requirements and energy-intensive cooling systems. The company plans to use modular computing architecture, allowing AI hardware from different chip manufacturers to be integrated into its satellites. Starmind satellites will use large solar arrays to generate electricity for onboard AI computing systems. The computing modules will process data locally, while high-speed optical links will transmit information between satellites and back to Earth through Starlink. The satellites are expected to operate in sun-synchronous orbit, allowing them to benefit from extended exposure to sunlight and provide a steady source of solar power. SpaceX plans to use deployable liquid radiators and active cooling systems to manage the heat generated by computing hardware. Heat will be dissipated into space, reducing reliance on conventional cooling equipment such as chillers, cooling towers and fans used in terrestrial data centres. The company claims its space-based cooling architecture could reduce cooling power overhead by an order of magnitude. SpaceX's first satellite design for Starmind is called AI1. It is designed to combine onboard computing, solar power generation, thermal management and laser connectivity in a large orbital platform. The satellite will also feature micrometeoroid shielding and solar technology derived from SpaceX's existing satellite manufacturing capabilities. SpaceX is building the Gigasat Factory in Bastrop, Texas, to manufacture AI satellites at scale. The facility is expected to enable rapid production and deployment of thousands of AI satellites, with manufacturing targeted to begin as soon as late 2027. The company also plans to develop advanced AI chips through a fabrication facility being jointly developed with Tesla. Its modular architecture is intended to allow the integration and upgrading of next-generation processors. The constellation will primarily rely on high-speed optical laser links to interconnect satellites and transmit computing results through Starlink. The FCC authorisation also permits radio-frequency links for backup and emergency telemetry, tracking and command operations. These include the 18.8–19.3 GHz downlink and 28.6–29.1 GHz uplink bands, supplementing the satellite network's optical connectivity. The AI boom is driving demand for computing power, electricity, land and cooling infrastructure. Space-based data centres could offer an alternative by harnessing solar power in orbit and reducing dependence on terrestrial energy and cooling resources. However, the technology faces challenges, including launch costs, satellite maintenance, radiation exposure, data transmission, orbital congestion and space debris management. articles.title: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
articles.text:
US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space - BBC News
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, SpaceX is an aerospace company that builds rockets and spacecraft, as well as running satellite services US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind. The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy". However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky. There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections. SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities". FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth". "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said. Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world." Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results? Published 6 November Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back Published 20 November Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038. The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year. It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use. Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles). Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth. The plans to put data centres in orbit and on the Moon Published 10 April 2025 Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed. Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them. "That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said. Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision. It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky". It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky". Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet." Figure caption, The BBC visited Arizona before the US midterm elections to understand America's data-centre boom The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling. The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world. New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby. An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk. Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth. Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors. Illustration: Ajaya Mohanty The Centre has proposed a 50 per cent increase in Lok Sabha seats for every state and Union territory, and in the strength of their Legislative Assemblies, to implement one-third reservation for women, with the revised seat allocations and constituency boundaries to remain in place until 2051. The Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026, slated for introduction in the Lok Sabha on Monday, seeks to raise the House's maximum strength to 850, with up to 815 members from states and 35 from Union territories. It also proposes to raise the ceiling on the size of a state Assembly from 500 to 650. "The objective of the present Bill is to give immediate effect to one-third reservation for women, including women belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, in the House of the People and the Legislative Assemblies of the states and the Union territories, through a delimitation exercise," the Bill's Statement of Objects and Reasons says. It says the exercise "shall provide for an increase of 50 per cent in the number of seats in the House of the People and the Legislative Assemblies of the states and Union territories, over and above the number of seats existing immediately before such delimitation". The Bill adds that the quota would run for 15 years from the commencement of the 2023 amendment, with Parliament empowered to extend it by law. Parliament would also determine the authority and manner for rotating the seats reserved for women. The 2023 women's reservation law ties the quota's rollout to delimitation after publication of figures from the first census taken after that law comes into force. The new Bill would trigger the quota after the first delimitation under the proposed amendment, using the latest published census figures available at its commencement to redraw constituency boundaries. The Statement of Objects and Reasons says "the allocation of seats and the division into territorial constituencies so readjusted" would "continue until the year 2051". Thirupparankundram row: orders Karthigai Deepam to be lit on November 28; issues contempt notice The court made clear that its order was only limited to contempt petitions By Krishnadas Rajagopal Updated - November 27, 2026 at 08:31 PM. | NEW DELHI × Share WhatsApp X Facebook LinkedIn Messenger Reddit Mail https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/news/thirupparankundram-row-orders-karthigai-deepam-to-be-lit-on-november-28-issues-contempt-notice/article71751645.ece Copy The main case on religious rights concerning the Thirupparankundram lamp-lighting row would be heard in the second week of January 2027 | Photo Credit: - Rejecting the Tamil Nadu government’s claim that it stayed aloof from the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy Temple management’s religious and customary decisions, the Supreme Court on Friday prima facie held that non-compliance with its November 20 order to light the Karthigai Deepam atop Thirupparankundram Hill’s stone pillar amounted to “flagrant and wilful disobedience” born of a “pre-meditated conspiracy” between the State and the temple trustees. A Bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M. Pancholi ordered the Board of Trustees of the temple to be suspended before appointing two former High Court judges — former Chief Justice of Meghalaya High Court S Vaidyanathan and former Madras High Court judge Justice V Parthiban — to act as Receivers. The court directed the Karthigai Deepam to be lit again on November 28 (Saturday), this time on the stone pillar, as was originally ordered on November 20. The Receivers have to ensure the ceremony is carried out in consultation with the temple Sthanikars. If the current flame is not burning at the Deepa Mandapam, the court said, independent arrangements have to be made to light it at the Deepathoon on November 28. However, the interim order would not grant any future equities in favour of any parties. The court made clear that its order was only limited to contempt petitions. The main case on religious rights concerning the Thirupparankundram lamp-lighting row would be heard in the second week of January 2027. The court allowed members of the public to light lamps on the Thiruppankundram Hill on November 28. Central forces would provide security. A 50-metre boundary around the dargah, located near the stone pillar, would be cordoned off. Access and rights of worshippers to the dargah would not be affected, the court ordered. The Bench issued show cause notices to the Tamil Nadu Chief Secretary, the State’s Director General of Police, Madurai District Collector and Police Commissioner, Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Commissioner and Deputy Commissioner, the chairperson, Executive Officer and trustees of the Subramaniswamy temple to respond on why contempt action should not be issued against them for “brazen, calculated, mutual” disobedience of the November 20 order of the Supreme Court. The court ordered them to be personally present on December 15, the next date of hearing. The Chief Secretary was directed to forthwith, and not later than 10 days, to file a personal affidavit explaining the “apparent disregard” shown by the State to perform its constitutional duty under Article 144 to obey a Supreme Court order. He was directed to provide details of the traffic of communication, including emails, call records, etc, between the State and district administration. One of the contempt petitioners had sought an enquiry into whether Government Ministers, including Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay, had any role to play in what happened on November 24. “No person, however high, can defy a Supreme Court order. Anybody who tries to do that, creates constitutional chaos. We will set this right… We will deal this with an iron hand,” Justice Kumar observed. The Bench said its order was not an “invitation for negotiation”. If there was any modification to be done, the court would do it. Justice Kumar said temple trustees and the State authorities cannot read discretion or leeway into a Supreme Court order. The Bench said ‘justice’ was a Preambular value. The stream of justice cannot be polluted by defying a Supreme Court directive. Any attempt to do so would not be tolerated. Interpreting Supreme Court orders in silos or diluting them would amount to questioning the authority of the Supreme Court. Compliance instilled public confidence in the authority of the Supreme Court to administer justice, the Bench noted. “When this court speaks, it speaks with the authority of the Constitution. It has to be obeyed. The Executive authorities have wilfully disobeyed. This strikes at the very root of law. It has to be dealt with iron hands,” the court observed. The court said the District Collector was shedding “crocodile tears” with his version in a preliminary report that temple trustees refused to authorise a lamp lighting team and finally, lit the lamp at the “traditional” Deepa Mandapam. The contempt petitioners termed the temple trustees as “stooges” of their political bosses in the State. They said these trustees did not have the “guts” to defy a Supreme Court order on their own and pass a resolution to light the lamp at the Deepa Mandapam rather than the stone pillar. They submitted that the Collector’s claims that he did “everything under the sun to ensure compliance with the November 20 order” was bogus. “The State had already decided not to comply. The Board of trustee of the temple was chosen as the vehicle and refuge to hide behind. It was the weakest link in the administrative and political chain to justify this action… The Collector’s report was a tell-tale passing of the buck… He is just taking umbrage under the resolution of the devasthanam,” senior advocate Guru Krishnakumar submitted. He was joined in by senior advocates P Valliappan and J Saideepak Iyer. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, for the Archaeological Survey of India, suggested a neutral agency to manage the temple. The court said the contempt petitioners’ arguments and the responses of the State invokes a sense of pain and anguish. It summarised the feeling in one word, “alas”. Justice Kumar said it was hard to believe the Collector could not have done anything with the kind of powers he wielded within the district. The court expressed dissatisfaction with his report. The Bench said the facts prima facie show a serious infraction on the part of the temple trustees, aided by State authorities, which has undermined the authority of the court. “This has shocked the conscience of the court,” Justice Kumar said. articles.title: Karthigai Deepam row: SC issues contempt notice to Tamil Nadu officials
articles.text:
Karthigai Deepam row: SC issues contempt notice to Tamil Nadu officials | India News - Business Standard
Observing that the executive authorities in Tamil Nadu acted on the diktat of their political bosses, the Supreme Court on Friday issued a contempt notice to the Tamil Nadu chief secretary, DGP, Madurai collector and others over the violation of its November 20 Karthigai Deepam order. The top court suspended the board of trustees of Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy temple and ordered lighting of lamp at Thiruparankundram Deepathoon on Saturday using the flame lit at Uchaipillaiyar mandapam. Asking the Tamil Nadu chief secretary to appear personally, a bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi directed him to file an affidavit detailing emails, calls exchanged and messages exchanged between officials. "The wilful non-compliance of orders of the Court, especially by the executive authorities, cannot go unnoticed and it has to be dealt with an iron hand," the bench said. The top court also handed over the security of Tamil Nadu's Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy temple and Thiruparankundram hill to CRPF, citing the failure of the Tamil Nadu Police to implement its orders. The apex court said it cannot sit in a silo if its order is not complied with and added that its order is not an invitation to negotiate as it binds the State, its officers and every religious institution. It said any attempt to pollute stream of justice by any person, howsoever high he may be, will not be tolerated. The top court said the conduct of officers prima facie reveals a state of administrative chaos in Tamil Nadu. "The conduct alleged, as borne out by the record, would prima facie disclose a brazen and wilful disobedience of this Court's order, a flagrant disregard of the undertaking given before the High Court and a calculated affront to the authority of both constitutional courts," the bench said. On Wednesday, the Tamil Nadu government apologised to the top court over the non-lighting of the ceremonial lamp at Deepathoon and blamed the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy temple authorities for it. Despite the apex court's permission, the Karthigai Deepam was lit only at its customary Uchipillayar mandapam at Thirupparankundram on November 24 and not at Deepathoon. articles.title: NVIDIA reportedly halts AI chip shipments to Southeast Asia
articles.text:
NVIDIA Reportedly Halts AI Chip Shipments To Southeast Asia
Companies like Dell have stopped shipping server hardware to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. Sean Gallup/Getty Images Add Engadget on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover NVIDIA has reportedly put a stop to shipments of AI server hardware to four Southeast Asian countries. According to The Financial Times , a handful of the company's manufacturing partners, including Dell and Supermicro, told clients in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia that the chipmaker is not allowing their server orders to be sent to them. The Financial Times reports it's unclear if the halt is temporary. The news comes just days after NVIDIA reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive . In recent years, Chinese AI labs have turned to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia to gain access to NVIDIA's most powerful chips. They used a gap in US export controls by renting access through cloud compute providers that bought servers with NVIDIA GPUs inside. In recent weeks, the US Commerce Department moved to close that loophole. First by introducing new rules aimed at stopping that exact practice, and second by targeting Megaspeed, the company at the center of the NVIDIA scandal. On Wednesday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its "Entity List." Companies, including NVIDIA, now need a US license to ship goods covered by US export rules to Megaspeed. Huang had resigned from his position on November 12 after reports surfaced that he had engaged in multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive that some US officials suspect was a Chinese intelligence asset . Megaspeed had leased access to NVIDIA chips to Chinese companies. The Justice Department is also investigating whether Megaspeed broke US export rules . Under the new US rule, data centers that were already providing large amounts of computing power to companies based in China or other location covered by the rule have 90 days from November 19 to get a license if they want to keep doing so. "There's this new rule but no guidance on execution," one cloud executive told the outlet. "No one knows how to apply for this license while the 90-day clock is ticking. It's causing sheer chaos in the region." Demand from Chinese tech companies led to a data center construction boom in Southeast Asia. NVIDIA booked $104 billion in revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, representing a 72 percent increase from the year before.
